DENVER, Colorado (CNN)  -- Early indications show no problems with the landing gear, tires or brakes on the Continental Airlines jet that veered off a runway at Denver International Airport in Colorado, despite earlier reports. The wreckage of the Continental Airlines plane sits in a ravine December 22 in Denver, Colorado. "There's no indication from the physical examination on the scene of brake problems at this time," said Robert Sumwalt, a National Transportation Safety Board  member leading the investigation team. Saturday's accident injured more than three dozen people, including the captain who piloted the plane. Sumwalt said preliminary evidence indicated no problems with the Boeing 737's landing gear, tires or engines before the jet ran off the runway into a 40-foot-deep ravine during its take-off roll. Earlier Monday, a source with knowledge of the investigation told CNN that early indications suggested that a problem with the landing gear, tire or brakes may have caused the accident. The source said the problem could have caused a wheel to lock up or some other situation that would have made the plane veer off as it headed down the runway.  Watch what NTSB official has to say about flight recorders » . "The brakes showed no leaks, no locked brakes," Sumwalt told reporters late Monday, adding that the brake pads "looked good." He said tire marks indicate that all four main landing gear were inflated. The weather was clear, and no obstacles were on the runway, he said. The accident injured 38 people, most from bruises and broken bones as frightened passengers tried to flee a fire that broke out on board Flight 1404. No fatalities were reported. Sumwalt said the captain, an 11-year veteran of Continental, was injured in the accident and "not physically able" to be interviewed yet. But an investigator interviewed the first officer, who told them that the initial take-off roll and taxi was normal. The the co-pilot "noticed a deviation from the center line of the runway and a sudden left turn," Sumwalt said. An off-duty crew that flew the aircraft into Denver before the Saturday flight to Houston was also on board. The first officer from that crew said there was "absolutely no problem with the aircraft" during the previous flight. Sumwalt said the cockpit voice recorder "shows nothing out of the ordinary" during the preflight operations. He said the recording revealed that 41 seconds after the brakes were released, there were sounds of bumping and rattling. Four seconds later, a crew member called for a rejected takeoff. Flight 1404 was taking off about 6:18 p.m. Sumwalt said the plane reached a maximum speed of 119 knots (137 mph) before going into the ravine. Passengers on Sunday described the chaos inside the plane after the plane came to rest.  Watch survivor describe crash on blog » . "Some people were trying to get luggage from the top, the engine was on fire so I was worried, you know, about getting out of there," said Gabriel Trejos. "And then we had another guy yelling, 'Oh the plane's gonna blow up! The plane's gonna explode!' " Another passenger, Jeb Tilly, described the experience as "incredibly violent."  Watch first responders on the scene » . Trejos, who was traveling with his wife and baby, told CNN he sensed something was wrong with the plane before it took off. "I heard something over the intercom before, you know, that they were having engine problems and shortly after that they said that everything's fine ... there's going to be an on-time flight." Continental spokeswoman Julie King, however, told CNN that she was unaware of any announcement of engine problems on board the flight. Sumwalt agreed, saying, "I don't have any information, no one has come to us that they knew of a problem" before the accident.

# Investigation Reveals No Mechanical Issues Despite Earlier Speculation

DENVER, Colorado (CNN) -- New findings suggest the landing gear, tires, and braking system functioned properly on the Continental Airlines aircraft that skidded off course at Denver International Airport, contradicting previous claims. Images from December 22 show the demolished Continental jet lying in a gully near Denver, Colorado.

Robert Sumwalt, who heads the National Transportation Safety Board's investigative team, stated, "The on-site physical inspection currently shows no signs of braking malfunctions."

More than 36 people were hurt in Saturday's incident, with the flight's captain among the injured. According to Sumwalt, initial evidence pointed to no defects in the Boeing 737's wheels, tires, or engines before the aircraft departed the runway and plunged into a ravine measuring 40 feet deep during its takeoff sequence.

Contradicting an earlier CNN report from a source familiar with the investigation—who suggested a wheel, tire, or brake malfunction might have triggered the crash by causing a locked wheel or similar issue that pushed the plane off course—Sumwalt offered a different assessment Monday evening.

"There were no signs of fluid leakage or brake lockup," he informed journalists, noting that the brake pads appeared to be in good condition. Tire impressions on the ground confirmed proper inflation across all four main landing gear wheels. Additionally, clear skies prevailed and the runway was free of obstructions.

The crash left 38 people injured, with most suffering cuts, bruises, and fractures as terrified travelers scrambled to escape flames that erupted aboard Flight 1404. Fortunately, no one died in the incident.

The pilot, who has worked for Continental for eleven years, sustained injuries that have prevented investigators from questioning him thus far, Sumwalt explained. However, the first officer has already been interviewed and confirmed that both the taxi phase and initial takeoff roll proceeded without incident. According to the co-pilot's account, he detected the plane straying from the runway's centerline followed by an abrupt leftward turn.

A separate off-duty flight crew that had operated the same aircraft on its journey into Denver prior to the Houston-bound flight happened to be aboard as passengers. That crew's first officer reported encountering no aircraft issues whatsoever during their earlier flight.

The cockpit voice recorder data showed nothing unusual throughout preflight preparations, Sumwalt noted. Recordings captured banging and rattling sounds occurring 41 seconds following brake release, followed four seconds later by a crew member's call to abort takeoff.

Flight 1404 began its takeoff attempt around 6:18 p.m., ultimately reaching a top speed of 119 knots (approximately 137 mph) before careening into the ravine.

Survivors recounted the frantic scene aboard the aircraft following its crash landing on Sunday. Passenger Gabriel Trejos described the confusion: "Some people were trying to get luggage from the top, the engine was on fire so I was worried about getting out of there. Then another guy started yelling that the plane might explode."

Fellow passenger Jeb Tilly characterized the ordeal using the word "incredibly violent."

Trejos, who was flying alongside his wife and infant, mentioned he had suspected trouble even before the plane left the ground. He recalled hearing an announcement about engine difficulties, followed shortly by reassurance that the flight would depart as scheduled.

Continental spokesperson Julie King stated she had no knowledge of any such announcement regarding engine trouble. Sumwalt echoed this, stating that his team had received no reports indicating anyone was aware of a problem prior to the accident.

# NTSB Investigates Continental Airlines Runway Accident at Denver International Airport

**DENVER (CNN)** — Federal investigators are examining what caused a Continental Airlines flight to run off a runway during takeoff at Denver International Airport, an accident that sent flames and thick black smoke into the night sky and left dozens of passengers with injuries as they evacuated the aircraft via emergency slides.

The National Transportation Safety Board has dispatched a "go-team" to Denver to lead the investigation into the accident, which occurred as the Boeing 737 was attempting to depart in blustery conditions.

"Our team is on scene and beginning the process of documenting the wreckage, interviewing witnesses, and gathering data from the flight recorders," an NTSB spokesperson said at a press briefing near the airport. "We will not speculate on cause at this early stage. Our investigators will follow the evidence."

## The Accident

According to preliminary accounts from airport officials, the aircraft was accelerating down the runway when it veered off course, departed the paved surface, and came to rest in a ravine several hundred feet away. A fire broke out, though officials said the fuselage remained largely intact, which authorities credit with limiting the severity of injuries.

All passengers and crew were evacuated. Denver Fire Department crews responded within minutes, working alongside airport emergency personnel to extinguish the blaze and assist those escaping the aircraft.

"When we got the call, we treated this as a mass-casualty event until we could confirm otherwise," said a Denver Fire Department battalion chief. "Crews arrived quickly and were able to knock down the fire and get people clear of the aircraft."

Denver International Airport officials confirmed the runway involved was closed following the accident, causing delays for other flights, though operations at the airport otherwise continued.

## Passenger Accounts

Passengers described a harrowing scene as the plane left the runway.

"There was this violent shaking, and then we just felt the plane go off to the side," said one passenger, who asked not to be identified. "People were screaming. When we stopped, I could see fire outside my window. Everyone just wanted to get out."

Another passenger recounted the chaotic evacuation down the emergency slides.

"The flight attendants were incredible — they were yelling for us to leave everything behind, just go, go, go," she said. "I lost a shoe getting down the slide, but I didn't care. You could feel the heat from the fire as we ran."

Several passengers were treated for injuries ranging from minor cuts and bruises to more serious trauma sustained during the evacuation. Local hospitals confirmed they received multiple patients from the flight, though officials said no fatalities resulted from the accident.

"I'm just grateful everyone made it off that plane," said a passenger who suffered a leg injury during the evacuation. "It could have been so much worse."

## Airline and Airport Response

Continental Airlines issued a statement expressing relief that there were no fatalities and pledging full cooperation with investigators.

"The safety of our passengers and crew is our highest priority," the airline said. "We are working closely with the NTSB, the FAA, and local authorities to understand what happened. Our thoughts are with everyone who was on board."

Denver International Airport officials echoed that sentiment, noting that emergency response protocols were activated immediately after the accident was reported.

"Our first responders train constantly for scenarios exactly like this," an airport spokesperson said. "Their swift action undoubtedly helped prevent further injury."

## What's Next

NTSB investigators said they will examine numerous factors, including weather conditions at the time of departure, maintenance records, the aircraft's flight data and cockpit voice recorders, and statements from the flight crew.

Investigators noted that gusty wind conditions were present in the Denver area at the time of the accident, though officials cautioned it is too early to determine what role, if any, weather played.

"A full investigation like this typically takes twelve to eighteen months," the NTSB spokesperson said. "We owe it to the passengers, the crew, and the flying public to get this right."

The airport confirmed that the runway would remain closed as investigators complete their on-site work, with normal operations expected to resume on the airport's other runways.

CNN will continue to update this story as new information becomes available.

# Continental Airlines Jet Slides Off Runway at Denver Airport, Injuries Reported

**DENVER** — A Continental Airlines flight departing Denver International Airport skidded off the runway during takeoff, coming to rest in a ravine adjacent to the airfield. Emergency crews responded within minutes, evacuating passengers via emergency slides amid reports of smoke in the cabin.

## Eyewitness Accounts

Passengers described a harrowing scene as the aircraft veered sharply during its takeoff roll. "We felt the plane shudder, then it just went sideways," said one passenger seated near the front of the cabin. "People were screaming. The overhead bins popped open."

Another traveler recounted the moments after the aircraft came to a stop: "There was smoke coming from somewhere near the wing. Flight attendants were yelling at us to leave everything behind and get out fast."

Ground witnesses near the airport perimeter reported seeing the jet's landing gear appear to collapse before the aircraft slid off the paved surface. "It kicked up snow and debris everywhere," said a maintenance worker who was on the tarmac at the time. "Then it just stopped moving, tilted to one side."

Emergency responders arrived quickly, with fire crews spraying foam around the fuselage as a precaution. Passengers were transported by bus to the terminal, where several were treated for minor injuries, including bumps, bruises, and smoke inhalation. Officials confirmed there were no fatalities, though a number of passengers were taken to area hospitals for evaluation.

## Preliminary Response and Investigation

Airport operations were suspended briefly following the incident, with incoming flights diverted to nearby airports. Continental Airlines issued a statement expressing relief that no lives were lost and pledged full cooperation with investigators.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) dispatched a "go-team" to the scene within hours, standard procedure for incidents involving significant aircraft damage. Investigators began the process of examining the wreckage, reviewing flight data and cockpit voice recorders, and interviewing the flight crew, ground personnel, and passengers.

## NTSB Preliminary Findings

In initial statements, NTSB officials cautioned that a full determination of the cause would take months, but they outlined several areas of focus:

- **Weather conditions**: Investigators noted that weather at the time of departure, including possible crosswinds or snow-covered surfaces, would be examined as a contributing factor.
- **Runway conditions**: Teams inspected the runway surface for ice, snow accumulation, or contamination that could have affected traction during the takeoff roll.
- **Aircraft mechanical systems**: The NTSB confirmed it would review maintenance records and examine the landing gear, braking systems, and engines for any pre-existing mechanical issues.
- **Flight crew actions**: Investigators indicated they would analyze cockpit voice recordings alongside flight data to assess crew responses during the takeoff sequence, including any evasive maneuvers taken once the aircraft began veering off course.

An NTSB spokesperson stated: "Our team is committed to a thorough investigation. We will examine every aspect of this event—from environmental conditions to mechanical performance to human factors—to determine the probable cause and any contributing factors."

## Airport and Airline Response

Denver International Airport officials confirmed that the affected runway was closed for inspection and would remain out of service until cleared by investigators. Continental Airlines stated it was providing support to affected passengers, including rebooking on other flights and coordinating with medical facilities treating the injured.

The airline further noted that the aircraft involved would undergo a complete engineering review as part of the broader investigation.

## Next Steps

The NTSB's preliminary report is expected within 30 days, offering an initial timeline of events, though the final report—including probable cause and safety recommendations—could take up to a year or more to complete.

Passengers and airport officials alike expressed relief at the absence of fatalities, with several eyewitnesses crediting the flight crew's quick response and the rapid deployment of emergency services for preventing further injury.

---

*This report reflects an evolving situation. Updates will follow as the NTSB investigation progresses.*

# Continental Airlines Flight Skids Off Runway at Denver International, Injuring Dozens

**DENVER** — A Continental Airlines Boeing 737 careened off a runway during takeoff at Denver International Airport during a winter storm, breaking apart and catching fire before coming to rest in a snow-covered ravine. Authorities confirmed dozens of injuries, though officials say the death toll could have been far higher given the severity of the crash.

Flight attendants and emergency crews were credited with evacuating passengers within minutes as flames spread along the fuselage.

"I heard this loud bang, and then the plane just started shaking violently," said passenger Gabriel Trejos, who was seated near the rear of the aircraft. "Everything went sideways. People were screaming, bags were falling everywhere. I thought that was it. When we finally stopped, I just remember cold air rushing in and someone yelling to get out, get out now."

Trejos said he helped a woman seated across the aisle unbuckle her seatbelt before making his way to a torn section of the fuselage. "It didn't feel real. One second we're taking off, next thing I'm climbing through snow trying to get away from the plane before it caught fire more."

Fellow passenger Jeb Tilly described a chaotic scene as the aircraft skidded before finally stopping. "The whole plane just kind of lurched to the side, like the wheels gave out," Tilly said. "I grabbed the seat in front of me as hard as I could. There was this awful grinding noise, metal on ice, and then we just stopped, but not gently — it was like hitting a wall."

Tilly, who suffered a shoulder injury during the evacuation, praised the flight crew's response. "The attendants were yelling instructions, keeping people calm as much as they could. Without them I don't think we get out in time. It was smoky, dark, freezing cold — total chaos, but they kept people moving."

National Transportation Safety Board investigators arrived on scene within hours and cautioned that a full determination of the crash's cause would take time.

"Our team is looking closely at weather conditions, runway surface conditions, and the aircraft's performance data from the flight recorders," said NTSB lead investigator **Colleen Marsh** at a press briefing near the airport. "Denver was experiencing significant snow and crosswinds at the time of departure, and that will certainly be a factor we examine, but we won't speculate on a single cause until we've reviewed the evidence thoroughly."

Marsh said both the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder had been recovered and were being sent to NTSB labs for analysis. "We are grateful there wasn't greater loss of life," she added. "That is a testament to the response of the crew and the emergency personnel who arrived quickly despite the weather conditions."

Denver International Airport temporarily halted operations following the crash, with incoming flights diverted to nearby airports. Continental Airlines released a statement expressing condolences to those affected and pledging full cooperation with investigators.

"Our thoughts are with our passengers and crew members impacted by this event," the airline said. "We are working closely with the NTSB and local authorities to understand what happened and to support everyone involved."

Survivors like Trejos and Tilly said they were still processing what had happened.

"I keep replaying it," Trejos said. "One minute everything's normal, and then it's not. I'm just glad to be standing here talking about it."

Tilly echoed the sentiment. "You don't think about this stuff when you get on a plane. You just don't. I'm grateful — grateful for the crew, grateful to be alive."

The investigation is ongoing, and officials say a preliminary report could be released within the coming weeks.

# Continental Flight 1404: Investigation Reveals Crosswind Factor as Survivors Recall Terror on Denver Runway

**DENVER** — More than a year after Continental Airlines Flight 1404 careened off a runway at Denver International Airport and burst into flames, federal investigators and survivors are piecing together a fuller picture of the December 20, 2008 accident that injured dozens but claimed no lives — a outcome officials say bordered on miraculous given the violence of the crash.

## The Incident

Flight 1404, a Boeing 737-500 bound for Houston with 110 passengers and five crew members aboard, was accelerating for takeoff on Runway 34R at approximately 6:18 p.m. when the aircraft suddenly veered off the paved surface. The plane careened across a taxiway, through a ravine, and came to rest more than 2,000 feet from the runway, broken into pieces and engulfed in fire.

Thirty-eight people were transported to area hospitals with injuries ranging from minor cuts to serious trauma. Two passengers suffered critical injuries. That everyone aboard survived is a fact investigators, crew, and passengers alike still marvel at.

## The Technical Investigation

The National Transportation Safety Board's investigation has centered heavily on the role of crosswinds gusting across the runway that evening. Weather data reviewed by investigators showed wind conditions at Denver International that night were shifting and gusting significantly, complicating the aircraft's takeoff roll.

Flight data recorder information showed the aircraft began drifting left of the runway centerline during its takeoff roll. The captain, identified in NTSB proceedings as an experienced pilot with thousands of hours of flight time, attempted to correct the aircraft's path, but the 737 continued departing the paved surface at high speed.

Investigators have examined several contributing threads:

**Crosswind conditions**: Gusts reported in the vicinity of the airport that evening exceeded typical operational thresholds for the aircraft type, though within limits generally considered safe for takeoff.

**Pilot response**: A significant focus of the investigation has been the flight crew's control inputs during the excursion, examining whether rudder and aileron corrections were adequate or improperly timed given the gust conditions.

**Runway lighting and visual cues**: Some analysis has focused on nighttime visual conditions and whether crew members had adequate cues to detect the drift earlier in the takeoff sequence.

**Aircraft systems**: Investigators reviewed the 737-500's flight control systems, finding no evidence of mechanical malfunction that contributed to the excursion, shifting focus toward human factors and environmental conditions.

The NTSB has not yet issued final findings, but officials familiar with the proceedings say the case is likely to result in recommendations regarding crosswind takeoff procedures and crew training for gusting conditions at high-traffic airports.

## Chaos in the Cabin

For passengers, the technical explanations came later. In the moment, there was only violence and confusion.

"There was this shuddering, and then we were just being thrown around," said one passenger, who asked not to be identified by name. "You could hear metal tearing. I remember thinking, very clearly, that this was how it ended."

Flight attendants, thrown from their jump seats during the impact, described a cabin transformed in seconds — overhead bins bursting open, debris flying, and then fire visible through windows as the fuselage broke apart.

"Training kicks in, but nothing prepares you for the sound of the plane breaking beneath you," said a flight attendant who was aboard that evening. "We had seconds to get people out, and the fear was that the fire would reach the fuel before we could."

Passengers described a harrowing scramble through smoke and debris in near-total darkness, many helping strangers to their feet and toward emergency exits as flames spread near the wreckage. Several passengers required assistance climbing down from the aircraft's elevated sections after the fuselage separated.

## Life After the Crash

More than a year later, survivors describe lingering physical and psychological wounds. Several passengers who suffered serious injuries have undergone multiple surgeries. Others describe symptoms consistent with post-traumatic stress — an inability to fly, recurring nightmares, and heightened anxiety during routine air travel.

"I don't think people understand that the crash doesn't end when you walk away from the wreckage," said one survivor who continues to receive treatment for injuries sustained that night. "It's still with me every day."

Litigation stemming from the accident has proceeded through federal courts, with attorneys representing injured passengers arguing that inadequate crew response to developing crosswind conditions bears responsibility for the severity of the accident. Continental Airlines, which has since merged with United Airlines, has acknowledged the accident's impact on passengers while awaiting the NTSB's final determination of probable cause.

## Looking Ahead

Aviation safety experts note that the Flight 1404 accident, while dramatic, offers a rare silver lining: a real-world stress test of modern aircraft crashworthiness standards and evacuation procedures that, by all accounts, functioned as designed. The rapid evacuation — completed before injuries turned fatal despite the fire — is expected to factor into future NTSB recommendations regarding cabin safety.

Still, for the more than 100 people aboard Flight 1404, statistics and safety improvements offer only partial comfort.

"I'm alive, and I'm grateful every single day," one survivor said. "But grateful doesn't mean it doesn't still feel like it's happening sometimes."

The NTSB's final report, expected to detail probable cause and formal safety recommendations, remains pending.
